title: Semi-Ordered Permutation
statement:
`nums` is a permutation of length `n`: it contains each integer from `1` to `n` exactly once. Call it semi-ordered when its first element is `1` and its last element is `n`; the elements in between may be in any order.

One operation swaps two neighbouring elements of `nums`. Return the fewest operations needed to make `nums` semi-ordered (`0` if it already is).
constraints: nums is a permutation of 1 to n
notes:
## Intuition

Only two values matter: `1` must reach index `0` and `n` must reach index `n - 1`. A neighbour swap moves any one element by at most one position, so `1` needs at least `first` swaps and `n` needs at least `n - 1 - last`. Moving them separately achieves exactly that sum, unless their paths cross: when `1` starts to the right of `n`, at some point they sit side by side and a single swap moves both toward their goals, saving one operation. A brute force could search all arrangements breadth-first, but that explodes factorially.

## Approach

1. Let `n` be the length, `first` the index of `1` and `last` the index of `n`.
2. Count `moves = first + (n - 1 - last)`: the distance each value must travel.
3. If `first > last`, the two meet on the way and one swap serves both, so subtract one.
4. Return `moves`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [2, 1, 4, 3]`, `n = 4`:

- `first = 1` (the `1` is at index 1) and `last = 2` (the `4` is at index 2).
- `moves = 1 + (4 - 1 - 2) = 2`.
- `first > last` is false, so nothing is saved and the answer is `2`.

In Example 2, `[2, 4, 1, 3]` has `first = 2` and `last = 1`: the sum is `2 + 2 = 4`, and because `1` lies right of `4` one swap is shared, giving `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): two linear searches.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Forgetting the shared swap when `1` is to the right of `n` overcounts by one.
- The largest value is `n = nums.length`, not 50; search for `nums.length`.
- Check the smallest crossing case: `[2, 1]` gives `1 + 1 - 1 = 1`, a single swap that fixes both ends at once.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums`, which is also its largest value |
| `first` | index where `1` currently sits |
| `last` | index where `n` currently sits |
| `moves` | number of neighbour swaps needed |

narration.3: Find where 1 is; it has to travel left to index 0.
narration.4: Find where n is; it has to travel right to index n - 1.
narration.6: Each swap moves a value one step, so add the two travel distances.
narration.7: If 1 starts to the right of n, their paths cross.
narration.8: At the crossing one swap moves both of them, so one operation is saved.
narration.10: That is the fewest swaps that put 1 first and n last.
